title: Building this site with an AI-assisted feedback loop
summary: How I used Cursor, GPT-4o screenshot feedback and later an AI coding assistant to build and redesign this site, and what kept it honest: one data source, shared components and explicit checks.
lead: I work mostly on backend and AI systems, and I wanted a personal site without turning CSS into a side project. I built the first version with Cursor and screenshot feedback from GPT-4o. In this post I walk through that loop, the later redesign that moved the site onto shared article components and one JSON data source, and the checks I now use to tell what I have and have not verified.

graph LR

sections.title: Context: I build backends and avoid CSS
paragraphs: My day-to-day work is FastAPI services, retrieval and agent workflows. Layout and styling are the parts I would rather delegate, but I wanted a site that looked deliberate. I treated the interface as a feedback problem: if I could show a model what the page looked like and say what was wrong, I could make small, checkable changes without a design background.

I made the first commit on 26 March 2025 and built most of the first version over the following days. In my original post I described going from asking how to center a div to building most of the interface components in about two weeks. That is my own recollection; the commit dates are the only part anyone else can check.
I had no design files and no reference boards. My only design inputs were screenshots of my own work and the model's comments on them.

definitions.text: Next.js 14 with the App Router and TypeScript. I pinned next 14.2.4.
Tailwind CSS, and later DaisyUI theme tokens. Utility classes are easy for an AI tool to generate and easy for me to review in a diff.
Cursor, an editor with integrated AI coding assistance. I used it to write and restyle components.
GPT-4o, which accepts a screenshot and can comment on layout, typography and hierarchy.

sections.title: Make feedback concrete enough to act on
paragraphs: I put every component through the same loop: write or restyle it in Cursor, look at it in the browser, capture a screenshot, ask GPT-4o for design feedback with a stated goal, apply the suggestions, and repeat until the changes between iterations became small.

I learned quickly that the result was only as good as my feedback. Asking to make a page look better left too much open. A screenshot plus one specific observation made the next change small: a heading has too little contrast, the content column is too wide, or the mobile header overflows the viewport.

The model could also point at an actual element in the image instead of guessing from my description. After enough iterations I started noticing alignment and spacing problems myself, before the model mentioned them.

diagrams.chart:
graph TD

    B --> C["Capture a screenshot"]

steps.title: Write the component
steps.text: I started with something basic such as a hero, a card or a navigation bar, highlighted the weak parts and asked Cursor to restyle them with Tailwind.

steps.title: Review in the browser
steps.text: I refreshed the page and compared the result with what I intended.

steps.title: Capture a screenshot
steps.text: A full-page or section screenshot told the model more than any description I could write.

steps.title: Ask for design feedback
steps.text: I sent the screenshot with a goal, for example a more technical, terminal-inspired look.

steps.title: Apply the suggestions
steps.text: What came back in the first build: monospaced fonts, a blinking cursor beside my name, hover states.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: I stopped when the change between iterations became small.

sections.title: Example: the hero section
paragraphs: My first hero had a plain heading, default paragraph styling, a button without hover states and no visual hierarchy. When I showed GPT-4o a screenshot, it suggested more spacing and padding around the content, varied font weights to establish hierarchy, a subtle background treatment, hover effects on the button and a small visual element.

After three iterations the section had purposeful spacing, varied typography and light animation. Two of the changes I would not have thought of myself: the subtle background gradient and a secondary button to create hierarchy. I did not keep screenshots of that first version, so the image below shows the current, redesigned home page.

When I redesigned the site later, I kept the decisions that already worked: the emerald light theme and the blue and slate dark theme stayed, and typography, spacing and hierarchy carried the improvement.

figures.alt: Home page of the current site in light mode, with a terminal-style header, a round portrait, the name Minh Bui, the title Senior Applied AI Engineer and two buttons
figures.caption: My home page today, in light mode. The name, title and a one-sentence summary come before two actions, Experience and projects and View CV, with a plain link to the blog below them. This is the redesigned version, not the original hero.

sections.title: The loop covers visuals, not everything
paragraphs: Screenshot feedback helped with how a page looked, and with nothing else. My git history has a run of 14 commits titled fix bug vercel, 13 of them on 29 March 2025 and one on 30 March. That is what getting my first deployment to build looked like. A screenshot of a correct local page told me nothing about a failing build on the host.

Content had the same gap. A model can comment on hierarchy, but it cannot see in a screenshot whether a claim in a project description is true. That is why, in the later work, I moved verification out of the visual loop and into explicit data and checks.

sections.title: Replace one-off styling with shared article components
paragraphs: My original posts each carried their own markup and styling. For the redesign I introduced a shared article system in src/components/post: a header, a lead paragraph, callouts, code blocks, figures, steps, definition lists, tables, pull quotes, a Mermaid wrapper and a references list. I wrote the rules down in docs/blog-style-guide.md: neutral surfaces, one accent colour, no emoji, alt text and a caption for every image, and Mermaid diagrams with quoted labels and no custom colours.

I did this for maintenance. A post is now mostly content, and consistency in light and dark mode comes from one place instead of from each page. My project stories, including this one, are JSON files in src/content/project-stories rendered by a single story component, so writing a new one is a content change rather than a new page.

An AI coding assistant did the implementation of the restyle, so the commit is authored by the assistant, and its message lists the shared components, the neutral light and dark tokens, the greyscale Mermaid theme and the rewritten posts.

sections.title: Give content a single source of truth
paragraphs: I keep profile, experience, project, skill, education and certificate data in JSON files under src/db, separate from the components that render them. Updating my About page is a content change instead of a search for repeated text in markup.

The same files feed my CV. scripts/build_resume.py reads them and writes the PDF, a preview image and a manifest to public/resume. A second mode, npm run resume:check, recomputes a hash over the source files and the script, compares it with the manifest, then extracts text from the PDF and checks that every experience and selected project bullet appears in it. If I change the data and forget to rebuild the PDF, the check fails.

I chose a generated, checked PDF over recreating the document in the visitor's browser. The reviewed file is the file people download, so the preview and the download cannot drift apart, and the site does not need to load a PDF library for visitors.

sections.title: Treat the portfolio and the resume as different documents
paragraphs: A profile refresh exposed a mistake I had made: when I chose a short project list for the CV, I also removed older projects from my About page. The fix was architectural as well as editorial. About now renders every project, and each project carries a resume flag that only the PDF reads. My maintenance notes in docs/profile-and-resume.md say it in one line: set the flag to false for archive projects and never delete them to shorten the CV.

I now treat the two as documents for different readers. Someone scanning my CV needs the most relevant evidence quickly, within a fixed length. Someone visiting the portfolio may want the history, the implementation detail and a full write-up, such as this one.

sections.title: Review behavior as well as screenshots
paragraphs: After the redesign I reviewed the site at mobile, tablet and desktop widths (320, 390, 768 and 1280 pixels), covering navigation, theme persistence, section anchors and the PDF download path. That review found a header overflow that was not visible on desktop, and it confirmed that the downloaded PDF matched the committed file byte for byte. The production build generated all 17 pages.

These checks have limits. The Next.js configuration skips lint and type validation during builds, so a passing build is not a clean-repository result. ESLint passed for the files I changed, but repository-wide lint and type checks still report older failures in blog, demo, database and particle-background code. An embedded music player also reported a YouTube error during review, and external playback was not validated. The checks were local; I did not run them against a production deployment.

sections.title: Keep publishing and privacy explicit
paragraphs: My public CV carries professional profile links and no personal phone number or email address; the validator in the build script rejects contact fields and mailto or tel links. I keep full-contact copies outside the published directory, and I removed the old public PDF from the source tree.
Removing a file does not erase Git history or copies people have already downloaded, so I review artifacts before I push them. The screenshots in this post show only public site content.

sections.title: Limits and what I would change
paragraphs: I have no measurement of how much time the loop saved compared with another approach, and I would not claim one. The original post also proposed a local agent that would watch the dev server, capture screenshots on change and feed them to a model. That was an idea, and I have not built it. If I did, the first thing I would add is a stored set of screenshots per page and theme, so a change that breaks layout shows up as a diff instead of relying on my attention.

Two other things are on my list: turn lint and type checks back on in the build once the older files are fixed, and add a check that every project with an article link points to a page that exists. Both address the same weakness the loop has, which is that it only catches what someone happens to look at.

takeaways: A screenshot plus one specific observation produces smaller, more checkable changes than a general request to improve a page.
A visual feedback loop does not cover builds, deployments or the truth of written claims; those need their own checks.
One JSON source for the website and the CV, with a per-project flag for the short document, keeps the two from drifting apart.
Shared article components and a written style guide make consistency a property of the system instead of each page.
A passing build is not a clean result when lint and type checks are skipped, so say what was and was not checked.
reviewNotes: The original file had no date field. I set 2026-10-14 (the redesign date) because the story now covers that work. Use 2025-03-30 if you prefer the original post date, and confirm the intended publication date.
